questions.question: What are `io.Reader` and `io.Writer`, and why are they useful?
questions.title: The io.Reader and io.Writer contracts
questions.direct_answer: `io.Reader` supplies bytes through `Read(p []byte) (n int, err error)`, while `io.Writer` accepts bytes through `Write(p []byte) (n int, err error)`. Functions written against these small interfaces work with files, network bodies, compressors, buffers, and test doubles. That composition keeps algorithms independent of where data comes from or goes.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: A Reader fills part of a caller-provided byte slice.
A Writer reports how many supplied bytes it accepted.
Files, buffers, network bodies, and many wrappers implement these interfaces.
Algorithms can depend on capability instead of a concrete storage type.
The caller must still follow each interface's count-and-error contract.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`io.Reader` and `io.Writer` are the standard byte-stream boundaries in Go. Reader has one method that places up to `len(p)` bytes into caller-provided storage. Writer has one method that consumes bytes and reports the accepted count. Their small shape makes them easy for many unrelated types to implement.

An algorithm that accepts interfaces does not need separate versions for a file, HTTP response body, compressed stream, or in-memory buffer. Wrappers can also be stacked: a buffered reader can wrap a file, a decoder can wrap that reader, and the final parser sees only the capability it needs.

For example, a `copyText(dst io.Writer, src io.Reader)` helper can be tested with `strings.NewReader` and `bytes.Buffer`. Production code can call the same helper with two files. No filesystem mocking or type switch is necessary because both environments share the same contracts.

These interfaces describe streaming bytes, not closing, seeking, buffering, concurrency safety, or record boundaries. Ownership of a closer stays separate, and richer requirements use interfaces such as `io.ReadCloser` or `io.ReadSeeker`. I accept the smallest contract the function truly needs.

sections.title: Interface composition separates transport from transformation
sections.content:
The producer decides how bytes are obtained, the consumer decides what to do with them, and the algorithm between them knows only Read and Write. That separation is what lets standard helpers connect files, memory, compression, hashing, and networking.

Small interfaces do not remove protocol decisions. Text encoding, framing, limits, retries, and ownership still belong to the layer that understands them. Reader and Writer provide the plumbing, not the full application contract.

sections.title: Ask for capability, then add only required guarantees
sections.content:
A function that only reads should not require `*os.File`, because that unnecessarily demands filesystem identity and methods such as Chmod. Accepting `io.Reader` expands reuse and makes a deterministic memory test possible. If the function must close what it receives, that ownership should be explicit through `io.ReadCloser` or separate documentation.

Implementations may wrap one another without inheritance. `bufio.NewReader` accepts a Reader and returns another Reader with additional methods; gzip and hashing packages follow the same pattern. Each layer adds one behaviour while preserving the stream boundary.

sections.title: One algorithm, interchangeable endpoints
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[os.File] --> C[io.Reader input]
  B[strings.Reader] --> C
  C --> D[copyText algorithm]
  D --> E[io.Writer output]
  E --> F[os.File]
  E --> G[bytes.Buffer]
```

questions.question: How should a loop handle `Read` returning both data and an error?
questions.title: Processing Reader data before its error
questions.direct_answer: A Reader may legally return `n > 0` and a non-nil error in the same call, including data together with `io.EOF`. The loop must process `p[:n]` before reacting to the error. Treat EOF as normal completion after those bytes; return other errors after preserving any valid data already delivered.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Read examines only the first `n` bytes of the supplied buffer.
`io.EOF` means no more input after the delivered bytes.
A successful higher-level read commonly reports nil rather than EOF.
Avoid loops that test the error before consuming `n` bytes.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The Reader contract returns two independent pieces of information: how many bytes are valid now and what condition follows them. An implementation may return data and `io.EOF` together on its final call. The slice outside `p[:n]` is not part of that result and may contain old buffer data.

A correct manual loop handles `n > 0` first. It appends, parses, hashes, or writes those bytes, then inspects the error. `io.EOF` ends the loop normally; another error is returned after the already-delivered bytes have been accounted for.

For example, a Reader that returns `"last"` with `io.EOF` in one call is valid. Code that begins with `if err != nil { break }` loses the entire word. Code that consumes four bytes first and then checks EOF produces the complete output.

In most application code I prefer `io.Copy`, `io.ReadAll`, Scanner, or `io.ReadFull` because those helpers already implement the contract for a specific goal. When I write a manual loop, I also guard against broken readers that repeatedly return `0, nil` so the program does not spin forever.

sections.title: Count and error describe the same read boundary
sections.content:
The count answers what bytes are usable from this call. The error describes why the next read may not continue normally. Combining them lets an implementation return final data without requiring a separate empty read solely to announce EOF.

Higher-level helpers often consume EOF internally and return nil on successful completion. That is why callers should follow the documentation of the helper they invoke rather than applying one universal EOF branch everywhere.

sections.title: Order the loop around valid data
sections.content:
A robust order is Read, handle any positive count, then handle the error. The Reader documentation discourages returning `0, nil` when the buffer is non-empty because callers may interpret it as no progress; defensive loops can count repeated empty reads or use standard helpers that report `io.ErrNoProgress` where appropriate.

The same count-before-error idea appears in Writer results and network operations. Partial progress is observable and must not be discarded merely because the overall operation also failed.

sections.title: Correct order for one Read result
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[n, err = Read(buffer)] --> B{n > 0?}
  B -- Yes --> C[Process buffer[:n]]
  B -- No --> D{err?}
  C --> D
  D -- nil --> A
  D -- EOF --> E[Finish successfully]
  D -- other --> F[Return error after delivered data]
```

questions.question: What is a short write, and how should Go code handle it?
questions.title: Short writes and io.ErrShortWrite
questions.direct_answer: A short write occurs when `Write(p)` reports fewer than `len(p)` bytes accepted. The Writer contract requires a non-nil error in that case; `io.ErrShortWrite` represents an implementation that returned a short count without explaining why. Callers must inspect both count and error or use standard helpers that perform the necessary checks.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: A complete write has `n == len(p)` and a nil error.
`n < len(p)` is partial progress and requires a non-nil error.
`io.ErrShortWrite` names a short count with no explicit error.
Never assume one Write accepted the complete slice.
Use helpers such as `io.Copy` when they match the operation.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`io.Writer.Write` returns a byte count and an error because output can make partial progress. A conforming implementation must return a non-nil error when `n` is smaller than the input length. The caller may use the count to understand exactly how much was accepted before failure.

`io.ErrShortWrite` is the standard signal for an invalid or incomplete result where a writer accepted fewer bytes but returned no specific error. A wrapper or helper can convert that ambiguous result into a real failure instead of silently dropping the unwritten suffix.

For example, a deliberately broken writer can accept two bytes from `"hello"` and return `2, nil`. A safe one-shot helper compares the count with five and returns `io.ErrShortWrite`. Reporting success would produce truncated output that may remain unnoticed until data is parsed later.

Retrying a suffix is not automatically safe for every destination because an error can leave protocol or application state uncertain. I follow the writer's documented semantics and prefer standard operations such as `io.Copy` or a buffered encoder. Writer implementations themselves must never claim nil after a short acceptance.

sections.title: Partial progress is not success
sections.content:
The count identifies the accepted prefix of the input slice. The error explains why the operation stopped. Both values matter because output may already have changed even though the complete logical record was not written.

A nil error communicates that all supplied bytes were accepted. Code that ignores `n` trusts every Writer implementation to honour that promise, which can hide a broken custom wrapper or an unexpected boundary.

sections.title: Concept guide · Short writes and io.ErrShortWrite
sections.content:
A byte writer does not know whether one call represents a database record, an HTTP frame, or half a text line. If partial output makes the logical record invalid, the higher layer needs a recovery policy such as aborting the stream, replacing a temporary file, or closing the connection.

Implementers must not retain or modify the provided slice, even temporarily. Those rules let callers reuse buffers safely after Write returns and make wrappers composable. A correct adapter preserves counts and errors rather than replacing them with a misleading success.

sections.title: Interpreting Writer results
sections.content:
| Result | Meaning | Caller action |
|---|---|---|
| `n == len(p), err == nil` | Complete acceptance | Continue |
| `n < len(p), err != nil` | Partial progress with cause | Apply operation policy |
| `n < len(p), err == nil` | Broken or ambiguous short write | Return `io.ErrShortWrite` |
| `n > len(p)` | Invalid Writer result | Treat as implementation failure |
